title: Type 2 Diabetes: Diagnose, Risk-Stratify, Start the Right Initial Plan
bottomLine: Confirm diabetes using Canadian diagnostic criteria when the patient is stable and asymptomatic, but treat severe symptomatic hyperglycemia or metabolic decompensation immediately. Initial management combines education, lifestyle support, cardiovascular/renal risk assessment and pharmacotherapy matched to glycemic severity, comorbidity and patient priorities.
recognize: Polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision, recurrent infection and unintentional weight loss increase urgency.
A1C may be unreliable with altered red-cell turnover, hemoglobin variants or selected renal/hepatic conditions.
differentiate: Rapid weight loss, ketosis, younger age or autoimmune history can suggest type 1/LADA and make routine type 2 management unsafe.
Stress hyperglycemia during acute illness does not automatically establish chronic type 2 diabetes.
assessment: Assess symptoms, weight trajectory, BP, cardiovascular disease, HF, CKD/albuminuria, smoking, medications, hypoglycemia vulnerability, pregnancy and access/cost.
workup: Use A1C and/or plasma glucose criteria appropriately; confirm an isolated abnormal result in an asymptomatic patient and obtain baseline renal/cardiovascular complication/risk assessment.
management: Provide individualized nutrition/activity/self-management education and start pharmacotherapy according to glycemia and comorbidity. Metformin remains a common foundation, while specific SGLT2 inhibitors/GLP-1 receptor agonists may be indicated early for cardiorenal benefit independent of A1C.
medicationSafety: Severe symptomatic hyperglycemia, ketosis or hyperosmolarity requires insulin rather than slow outpatient tablet escalation.
Renal function, pregnancy, hypoglycemia risk, adverse effects and affordability alter drug choice.
redFlags: Rapid weight loss with marked hyperglycemia
counselling: Explain that treatment targets and drug selection are individualized and that cardiorenal-protective medication may be appropriate even when glucose is near target.
followUp: Review glycemia, medication tolerance, renal function and complication/risk-factor plan after initiation; intensify or de-intensify based on response.
examTrap: Waiting for a second outpatient diagnostic test before treating a symptomatic patient with ketosis or severe metabolic decompensation.
oneLinePearl: Confirm stable asymptomatic diabetes; treat metabolic decompensation now.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Definition, Classification and Diagnosis guidance
Diabetes Canada 2024 Type 2 pharmacologic management update

title: Type 1 Diabetes: Basal Insulin Is Never Optional
bottomLine: Type 1 diabetes is absolute insulin deficiency. Use physiologic basal-bolus or pump therapy, individualize carbohydrate/correction dosing and protect basal insulin during illness or fasting because complete insulin interruption can precipitate DKA quickly.
recognize: Polyuria/polydipsia, weight loss and ketosis may be the first presentation.
Pump interruption can cause rapid insulin deficiency because there is no long-acting depot.
differentiate: Type 2/ketosis-prone diabetes can also present with ketosis; antibody/C-peptide testing may help classification when the phenotype is unclear.
assessment: Review basal/bolus doses, carbohydrate strategy, CGM/pump data, hypoglycemia, injection/infusion sites, exercise, illness, psychosocial burden and access to supplies.
workup: Use A1C and glucose/CGM data for long-term control and ketone testing during significant hyperglycemia/illness; screen associated autoimmune/microvascular disease according to age/duration.
management: Use multiple daily injections or pump/automated insulin delivery with structured education and diabetes-team support. Adjust rather than omit basal insulin during NPO/illness according to the individualized plan.
medicationSafety: Insulin dosing errors can cause severe hypoglycemia; rapid-acting insulin timing must match carbohydrate/intake and current glucose.
Never stop all insulin in type 1 diabetes solely because the patient is not eating.
counselling: Teach sick-day rules, ketone testing, pump-failure backup, glucagon and driving/exercise hypoglycemia prevention.
followUp: Use regular diabetes-team review of glycemia, hypoglycemia, device use and psychosocial burden; reassess regimen after severe events.
examTrap: Holding all insulin because a person with type 1 diabetes is NPO.
oneLinePearl: No food may change the insulin dose; it does not remove the need for basal insulin.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Glycemic Management in Adults with Type 1 Diabetes

title: Diabetes Drugs Beyond Metformin: Choose for Heart, Kidney, Weight, and Hypoglycemia Risk
bottomLine: When adding or choosing therapy beyond metformin, the best drug is the one that fits cardiovascular/renal disease, glycemic need, hypoglycemia risk, weight goals, kidney function, adverse effects, cost/access and patient preference—not simply the largest expected A1C reduction.
recognize: Specific SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists provide cardiorenal benefit in indicated populations beyond glucose lowering.
Sulfonylureas and insulin have higher hypoglycemia risk, particularly with CKD, frailty or irregular intake.
differentiate: DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists are generally not combined routinely because they act on the same incretin pathway without meaningful added benefit.
The drug chosen for HF/CKD protection may differ from the drug chosen primarily for weight or glycemic potency.
assessment: Review ASCVD/HF/CKD/albuminuria, eGFR, weight goals, hypoglycemia risk, pancreatitis/gallbladder history, genital infections, cost/coverage, injections and pregnancy plans.
workup: Use A1C/glucose and renal/cardiovascular risk data; monitor class-specific renal, hydration or adverse-effect concerns rather than ordering one universal diabetes-drug panel.
management: Use individualized combination therapy and add cardiorenal-protective agents when indicated; de-intensify hypoglycemia-producing drugs when risk exceeds benefit.
medicationSafety: SGLT2 inhibitors require sick-day/perioperative holding in severe illness/fasting and awareness of euglycemic DKA; GLP-1 RAs can cause significant GI effects and class-specific contraindications; sulfonylureas can cause prolonged hypoglycemia.
counselling: Explain why a medication may be recommended for heart/kidney protection despite an acceptable A1C and review sick-day rules where relevant.
followUp: Reassess glycemia, tolerability, kidney function, weight and cardiorenal goals after changes.
examTrap: Choosing therapy solely from A1C potency while ignoring established HF/CKD or recurrent hypoglycemia.
oneLinePearl: Beyond metformin, choose the drug for the patient's outcomes—not just the glucose number.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada 2024 Pharmacologic Glycemic Management of Type 2 Diabetes update

title: Insulin Initiation and Titration: Basal First, Pattern-Based Adjustment
bottomLine: For most adults with type 2 diabetes adding insulin, start a low-dose basal regimen and titrate to fasting glucose while maintaining appropriate non-insulin therapies; add mealtime insulin stepwise when postprandial hyperglycemia remains. Severe symptomatic/metabolic decompensation is a different, more urgent insulin pathway.
recognize: Basal insulin primarily targets fasting/overnight hepatic glucose output.
Over-basalization is suggested when fasting glucose is controlled but A1C remains high and escalating basal insulin causes nocturnal/fasting hypoglycemia without fixing post-meal excursions.
differentiate: Basal insulin initiation in stable type 2 diabetes differs from basal-bolus therapy for type 1 diabetes or IV insulin for DKA/HHS/critical illness.
assessment: Review glucose pattern, meals, renal function, hypoglycemia history, cognitive/manual ability, vision, injection technique, cost, existing drugs and support system.
workup: Use fasting and postprandial glucose/CGM patterns to identify where insulin is needed; do not titrate from A1C alone.
management: Start basal insulin and titrate gradually to fasting target; when bolus insulin is needed, add it stepwise beginning with the meal causing the greatest excursion and reassess secretagogues/hypoglycemia-producing drugs.
medicationSafety: All patients starting insulin need hypoglycemia prevention/treatment education. Concentrated insulins and device changes require explicit dose/unit verification.
Illness, fasting and kidney decline can materially change insulin requirements.
redFlags: Rapid renal decline with falling insulin requirement
counselling: Teach injection/device technique, storage, glucose pattern review, hypoglycemia rescue and how titration instructions work.
followUp: Review frequently during titration until stable, then reassess A1C/patterns and treatment burden at appropriate intervals.
examTrap: Continuing to increase basal insulin when fasting glucose is already at target but post-meal glucose remains high.
oneLinePearl: Titrate the insulin component that matches the glucose pattern.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada 2024 Type 2 pharmacologic management update

title: CGM Interpretation: Time in Range, Patterns, and Sensor Context
bottomLine: CGM is interpreted as a pattern, not one sensor point. Review data sufficiency, time in range/below/above range, overnight/meal/exercise trends, variability and hypoglycemia exposure, then change therapy only after checking sensor context, meals, doses and behaviour.
recognize: CGM can reveal nocturnal or postprandial patterns missed by A1C and fingerstick snapshots.
Sensor glucose measures interstitial glucose and can lag during rapid change; symptoms that conflict with a reading may require confirmatory capillary testing depending on device/instructions.
differentiate: A1C summarizes average glycemia and can hide hypoglycemia/variability; CGM adds time-pattern information.
One low sensor value from compression/lag is not automatically true hypoglycemia, but symptomatic low readings should never be dismissed.
assessment: Review wear time/data completeness, insulin/medication timing, meals, activity, alcohol, illness, sleep and hypoglycemia awareness.
workup: Use standardized ambulatory glucose profiles and device metrics rather than scrolling isolated daily graphs; compare with A1C when discordance suggests altered red-cell turnover or sensor issues.
management: Prioritize reducing dangerous hypoglycemia, then address persistent fasting/postprandial patterns and variability; use alerts/automated insulin features with individualized education.
medicationSafety: Do not stack rapid-acting correction insulin repeatedly based on rapidly changing sensor arrows without accounting for insulin-on-board.
Confirm device-specific actions for suspected sensor failure or severe symptoms.
counselling: Teach trend arrows, alert fatigue management, compression lows and when a fingerstick/ketone check is needed.
followUp: Reassess patterns after medication/device changes and ensure the patient can use data without creating anxiety or unsafe overcorrection.
examTrap: Changing basal insulin because of one isolated CGM high rather than a reproducible overnight/fasting pattern.
oneLinePearl: CGM decisions come from repeated patterns and exposure—not a single dot.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Monitoring Glycemic Control and Type 1 Diabetes CGM resources

title: DKA: Ketosis and Acidosis, Potassium-Aware Insulin, Cause Control
bottomLine: DKA is insulin deficiency causing ketosis and metabolic acidosis with major water/electrolyte loss. Restore perfusion, know potassium before insulin, continue insulin until ketoacidosis resolves, add dextrose as glucose falls, and find the precipitant; SGLT2-associated and pregnancy DKA may occur at lower glucose levels.
recognize: Polyuria/polydipsia, vomiting/abdominal pain, dehydration, Kussmaul breathing, ketones and acidosis are typical.
Serum potassium may initially appear normal/high despite total-body potassium depletion.
differentiate: HHS has more profound hyperosmolar dehydration with less ketoacidosis; starvation/alcohol ketosis and lactic acidosis have different contexts.
assessment: Assess ABCs, mental status, perfusion, infection/ischemia, insulin omission/pump failure, pregnancy, SGLT2 use and potassium/ECG risk.
workup: Use glucose, electrolytes/renal function, beta-hydroxybutyrate/ketones, venous/arterial acid-base data and precipitant-directed testing; urine ketones alone can underrepresent beta-hydroxybutyrate-predominant DKA.
management: Use a validated protocol with isotonic fluids, potassium-guided IV insulin, dextrose when needed to continue clearing ketosis and treatment of the precipitating cause.
medicationSafety: Insulin can precipitate dangerous hypokalemia; severe potassium depletion must be corrected before insulin proceeds.
Do not stop insulin just because glucose normalizes if ketosis/acidosis persists.
counselling: After recovery teach sick-day insulin continuity, ketone testing, pump backup and SGLT2 hold rules.
followUp: Resolve medication/access/education/illness factors before discharge and arrange diabetes follow-up.
examTrap: Stopping IV insulin when glucose falls to target while ketoacidosis is still present.
oneLinePearl: DKA ends when ketosis/acidosis resolves—not when glucose looks normal.

title: HHS: Hyperosmolar Dehydration, Slow Correction, Find the Trigger
bottomLine: HHS is profound hyperglycemia/hyperosmolality with severe volume depletion and relatively little ketoacidosis. Restore volume carefully, monitor corrected sodium/osmolality and potassium, use insulin after initial fluid resuscitation as appropriate, and treat the precipitating illness while avoiding rapid osmotic shifts.
recognize: Older adults may present with marked dehydration, weakness, neurologic change or coma; infection, MI/stroke, medications and inadequate water access are common triggers.
HHS and DKA can overlap, especially in severely ill patients.
differentiate: HHS has greater hyperosmolality/water deficit and less ketosis than classic DKA; altered mental status should also trigger stroke/infection/drug differential.
assessment: Assess perfusion, mental status, volume loss, urine output, infection/ischemia/neurologic symptoms, medication access, baseline kidney/heart disease and ability to obtain water.
workup: Use glucose, electrolytes, renal function, measured/calculated osmolality, acid-base/ketones and precipitant-specific ECG/cultures/imaging.
management: Prioritize individualized fluid resuscitation, potassium/electrolyte monitoring and gradual osmolality correction; use insulin according to the validated HHS protocol and address infection/ischemia/other trigger.
medicationSafety: Rapid changes in glucose/osmolality can cause neurologic harm; HF/CKD require frequent fluid reassessment rather than fixed-volume reflexes.
counselling: After recovery review hydration access, medication adherence/sick-day plan and early hyperglycemia symptoms.
followUp: Ensure trigger and social/access barriers are addressed; follow renal/neurologic recovery and diabetes regimen.
examTrap: Treating HHS like DKA with glucose-focused insulin before addressing profound volume/osmotic physiology.
oneLinePearl: HHS is a water-and-osmolality emergency as much as a glucose emergency.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Hyperglycemic Emergencies in Adults

title: Hypoglycemia: Rescue the Low, Then Redesign the Risk
bottomLine: Treat hypoglycemia immediately, then prevent recurrence by finding the medication, meal, exercise, alcohol, kidney/liver, endocrine or access factor that caused it. A severe event is a regimen-safety failure until proven otherwise.
recognize: Adrenergic symptoms include tremor/sweating/palpitations; neuroglycopenia causes confusion, behaviour change, seizure or coma.
Older adults may present with falls, weakness or delirium and can have impaired warning symptoms.
differentiate: Conscious safe-swallow patients can use fast carbohydrate; severe hypoglycemia requiring help needs glucagon or IV glucose according to access/setting.
Sulfonylurea or long-acting insulin episodes can recur after initial correction.
assessment: Check glucose promptly without delaying rescue; assess airway/neurology/injury, insulin/secretagogue timing, meals, exercise, alcohol, renal/liver function, food security and awareness.
workup: Recurrent/unexplained hypoglycemia without an obvious diabetes-drug cause requires cause-directed endocrine/hepatic/renal/critical-illness evaluation.
management: Use Diabetes Canada rapid-carbohydrate treatment for conscious patients and external rescue for severe episodes; after recovery adjust/de-intensify the cause, restore longer-acting nutrition as appropriate and prescribe/teach glucagon for high-risk patients.
medicationSafety: Do not tell a patient with recurrent medication-induced lows simply to eat more; lower-risk therapy or dose/regimen redesign is often required.
Kidney decline can markedly reduce insulin/secretagogue requirements.
redFlags: Frailty/impaired awareness/living alone after severe event
counselling: Teach fast carbohydrate, glucagon, driving/exercise safety, CGM alerts where appropriate and an individualized prevention plan.
followUp: Every severe episode needs prompt medication review and follow-up; review CGM/SMBG patterns rather than waiting for the next event.
examTrap: Correcting the glucose and discharging without changing the regimen that caused recurrent severe hypoglycemia.
oneLinePearl: Rescue ends the episode; regimen redesign prevents the next one.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Hypoglycemia in Adults 2023 update
